Individual MAST30027 coursework, adapted for a portfolio. Assessment instructions are omitted.

```{r}
X <- scan("data/reef_counts_unlabelled.txt", quiet = TRUE)
X0 <- scan("data/reef_counts_labelled.txt", quiet = TRUE)
stopifnot(length(X) == 300, length(X0) == 100)
```

## Problem 1

### Part (a): Expected complete log-likelihood

For $k=1,2,3$, let $I(Z_i = k)$ denote the indicator that reef $i$ belongs to class $k$. Then the complete-data likelihood is
$$
P(X, Z\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{300}\prod_{k=1}^3
\left[
P(Z_i=k\mid\theta) P(X_i=x_i\mid Z_i=k,\theta)
\right]^{I(Z_i=k)}.
$$
Since $P(Z_i=k\mid\theta)=\pi_k$ and $X_i\mid Z_i=k\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_k)$,
$$
P(X,Z\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{300}\prod_{k=1}^3
\left[
\pi_k\frac{\lambda_k^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_k}}{x_i!}
\right]^{I(Z_i=k)}.
$$
Therefore, the complete-data log-likelihood is
$$
\log{P(X, Z\mid\theta)}=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^{3}I(Z_i=k)
\left[\log{\pi}_k+x_i\log{\lambda_k}-\lambda_k-\log{(x_i!)}\right].
$$
The expected complete log-likelihood is
$$
Q(\theta,\theta^0)=E_{Z\mid X,\theta^0} \left[\log{P}(X,Z\mid\theta) \right].
$$
Hence,
$$
Q(\theta, \theta^0)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^{3}E_{Z\mid X, \theta^0} [I(Z_i=k)]
[\log\pi_k+x_i\log\lambda_k-\lambda_k-\log(x_i!)].
$$
Define the responsibility
$$
\tau_{ik}^{0}= P(Z_i=k\mid X_i=x_i, \theta^0).
$$
Since
$$
E_{Z\mid X,\theta^0}[I(Z_i=k)]=P(Z_i=k\mid X_i=x_i,\theta^0)=\tau_{ik}^0,
$$
we obtain
$$
\boxed{
Q(\theta, \theta^0)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^{3}\tau_{ik}^{0}[\log\pi_k+x_i\log(\lambda_k)-\lambda_k-\log(x_i!)]
}
$$
Here, $\tau_{ik}^{0}$ is the posterior probability, under the current parameter values $\theta^0$, that reef $i$ belongs to class $k$.

### Part (b): E-step

In the E-step, we calculate the responsibilities
$$
\tau_{ik}^{0}=P(Z_i=k\mid X_i=x_i,\theta^0).
$$
Using Bayes' rule,
$$
P(Z_i=k\mid X_i=x_i, \theta^0)= \frac{P(Z_i=k\mid\theta^0)P(X_i=x_i\mid Z_i=k, \theta^0)}{\sum_{j=1}^{3}P(Z_i=j\mid\theta^0)P(X_i=x_i\mid Z_i=j,\theta^0)}.
$$
Substituting the mixture proportions and Poisson probability mass functions gives
$$
\tau_{ik}^{0}=\frac{\pi_k^0\frac{(\lambda_k^{0})^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_k^0}}{x_i!}
}{
\sum_{j=1}^{3}\pi_j^0\frac{(\lambda_j^{0})^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_j^{0}}}{x_i!}}.
$$
Since the factor $x_i!$ is common to all terms, it cancels:
$$
\boxed{\tau_{ik}^0=\frac{\pi_k^0(\lambda_k^0)^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_k^0}
}{\sum_{j=1}^3\pi_j^0(\lambda_j^0)^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_j^0}}}
\qquad k=1,2,3
$$
For one reef $i$, $\tau_{ik}^0$ is the current posterior probability that the reef belongs to management class $k$, given its observed count $x_i$.

### Part (c): M-step

In the M-step, the responsibilities $\tau_{ik}^0$ are treated as fixed, and we maximise $Q(\theta,\theta^0)$ with respect to $\theta$.

For the mixture proportions, we maximise
$$
\sum_{k=1}^3(\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0)\log\pi_k
$$
subject to
$$
\pi_1+\pi_2+\pi_3=1
$$
Using a Lagrange multiplier $\alpha$, define
$$
\mathcal{L}=\sum_{k=1}^3(\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0)\log\pi_k+\alpha\left(1-\sum_{k=1}^3\pi_k\right).
$$
Differentiating with respect to $\pi_k$,
$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\pi_k}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0}{\pi_k}-\alpha=0.
$$
Hence,
$$
\pi_k=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0}{\alpha}.
$$
Summing over $k=1,2,3$ and using $\sum_{k=1}^3\pi_k=1$,
$$
1=\frac{1}{\alpha}\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^3\tau_{ik}^0.
$$
Since $\sum_{k=1}^3\tau_{ik}^0=1$ for each reef $i$,
$$
\alpha=300.
$$
Therefore, the updated mixture proportions are
$$
\boxed{
\pi_k^{\text{new}}=\frac{1}{300}\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0
}\qquad k=1,2,3.
$$
For $\lambda_k$, retain the terms in $Q$ that depend on $\lambda_k$:
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0(x_i\log\lambda_k-\lambda_k).
$$
Differentiating with respect to $\lambda_k$,
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\lambda_k}=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0
\left(\frac{x_i}{\lambda_k}-1
\right).
$$
Setting this equal to zero gives
$$
\frac{1}{\lambda_k}\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0x_i=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0
$$
Hence,
$$
\boxed{
\lambda_k^{\text{new}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0}
}\qquad k=1,2,3.
$$
Thus, each updated $\pi_k$ is the average responsibility assigned to class $k$, while each updated $\lambda_k$ is the responsibility-weighted mean of the observed counts for that class.

### Part (d): Implementation

The incomplete log-likelihood for the three-component Poisson mixture is
$$
\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\log\left[\sum_{k=1}^3\pi_kf(x_i;\lambda_k)
\right].
$$
I implemented the EM algorithm using the E-step and M-step derived above. The algorithm stops when either the change in the incomplete log-likelihood is less than $10^{-5}$, or 100 EM iterations have been completed.

```{r}
compute.prob.x.z <- function(X, w.curr, lambda_curr) {
  
  prob.x.z <- matrix(
    NA,
    nrow = length(X),
    ncol = length(w.curr)
  )
  
  for (k in seq_len(ncol(prob.x.z))) {
    prob.x.z[, k] <- dpois(X, lambda_curr[k]) * w.curr[k]
  }
  
  return(list(prob.x.z = prob.x.z))
}

compute.log.lik <- function(X, w.curr, lambda_curr) {
  
  prob.x.z <- compute.prob.x.z(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)$prob.x.z
  ill <- sum(log(rowSums(prob.x.z)))
  
  return(list(ill = ill))
}

EM.iter <- function(X, w.curr, lambda_curr) {
  
  # E-step
  prob.x.z <- compute.prob.x.z(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)$prob.x.z
  
  P_ik <- prob.x.z / rowSums(prob.x.z)
  
  # M-step
  w.new <- colSums(P_ik) / sum(P_ik)
  
  lambda_new <- colSums(P_ik * X) / colSums(P_ik)
  
  return(list(w.new = w.new, lambda_new = lambda_new))
}
```

```{r}
mixture.EM <- function(X, w.init, lambda_init, epsilon = 1e-5, max.iter = 100) {
  w.curr <- w.init
  lambda_curr <- lambda_init
  
  log_liks <- c()
  log_liks <- c(
    log_liks,
    compute.log.lik(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)$ill
  )
  
  delta.ll <- Inf
  n.iter <- 1
  
  while ((delta.ll > epsilon) & (n.iter <= max.iter)) {
    EM.out <- EM.iter(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)
    
    w.curr <- EM.out$w.new
    lambda_curr <- EM.out$lambda_new
    
    log_liks <- c(
      log_liks,
      compute.log.lik(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)$ill
    )
    
    delta.ll <- abs(log_liks[length(log_liks)] - log_liks[length(log_liks) - 1])
    n.iter <- n.iter + 1
  }
  
  return(list(w.curr = w.curr, lambda_curr = lambda_curr,
              log_liks = log_liks, n.iter = n.iter -1))
}
```

```{r}
EM1 <- mixture.EM(X, w.init = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.4), lambda_init = c(3, 20, 35))

EM2 <- mixture.EM(X, w.init = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.7), lambda_init = c(5, 25, 40))
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Incomplete log-likelihood trajectories for the two EM initialisaitions."
ylim_range <- range(c(EM1$log_liks, EM2$log_liks))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(
  0:(length(EM1$log_liks) - 1),
  EM1$log_liks,
  type = "b",
  ylim = ylim_range,
  xlab = "Iteration",
  ylab = "Incomplete log-likelihood",
  main = "Initialisation 1"
)

plot(
  0:(length(EM2$log_liks) - 1),
  EM2$log_liks,
  type = "b",
  ylim = ylim_range,
  xlab = "Iteration",
  ylab = "Incomplete log-likelihood",
  main = "Initialisation 2"
)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```
```{r}
all(diff(EM1$log_liks) >= -1e-10)
all(diff(EM2$log_liks) >= -1e-10)

EM1$log_liks[length(EM1$log_liks)]
EM2$log_liks[length(EM2$log_liks)]

results <- rbind(
  EM1 = c(
    pi1 = EM1$w.curr[1],
    pi2 = EM1$w.curr[2],
    pi3 = EM1$w.curr[3],
    lambda1 = EM1$lambda_curr[1],
    lambda2 = EM1$lambda_curr[2],
    lambda3 = EM1$lambda_curr[3],
    logLik = EM1$log_liks[length(EM1$log_liks)],
    iterations = EM1$n.iter
  ),
  EM2 = c(
    pi1 = EM2$w.curr[1],
    pi2 = EM2$w.curr[2],
    pi3 = EM2$w.curr[3],
    lambda1 = EM2$lambda_curr[1],
    lambda2 = EM2$lambda_curr[2],
    lambda3 = EM2$lambda_curr[3],
    logLik = EM2$log_liks[length(EM2$log_liks)],
    iterations = EM2$n.iter
  )
)

round(results, 4)

```
For both initialisations, the incomplete log-likelihood increased monotonically at each EM iteration, as shown in the figure. Both runs converged after 12 iterations and attained essentially the same final incomplete log-likelihood, -1136.962.
The resulting parameter estimates were
$$
\hat{\pi}_1=0.291, \qquad \hat{\pi}_2=0.285, \qquad \hat{\pi}_3=0.424
$$
and
$$
\hat{\lambda}_1=5.91, \qquad \hat{\lambda}_2=20.43, \qquad \hat{\lambda}_3=37.98.
$$
Since both initialisations converged to essentially the same solution and achieved the same incomplete log-likelihood, either run gives the selected MLE estimates.
Thus, the fitted mixture suggests that approximately 29%, 29% and 42% of the reef-season observations belong to the three latent classes, with typical seasonal counts of about 6, 20 and 38 coral trout, respectively.

## Problem 2

### Part (a): Expected complete log-likelihood

For the first 300 observations, the class labels remain unobserved, so their contribution is the same as in Problem 1. For the 100 labelled observations, $X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_2)$ for $i=301, ..., 400$.

Therefore, the complete-data likelihood is
$$
P(X,Z\mid \theta) = \left\{\prod_{i=1}^{300}\prod_{k=1}^3\left[
\pi_k\frac{\lambda_k^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_k}}{x_i!}
\right]^{I(Z_i=k)}
\right\}
\left\{
\prod_{i=301}^{400}\frac{\lambda_2^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_2}}{x_i!}
\right\}.
$$
Taking logarithms,
$$
\log P(X,Z\mid\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^3I(Z_i=k)
\left[
\log(\pi_k)+x_i\log(\lambda_k)-\lambda_k-\log(x_i!)
\right]
$$
$$
+\sum_{i=301}^{400}\left[
x_i\log(\lambda_2)-\lambda_2-\log(x_i!)
\right].
$$
Hence,
$$
Q(\theta, \theta^0)=E_{Z\mid X, \theta^0}
\left[
\log P(X, Z\mid \theta)
\right].
$$
Since the second term contains no unobserved class indicators, it is unaffected by the expectation. Therefore,
$$
Q(\theta, \theta^0)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^3
E_{Z\mid X,\theta^0}
\left[I(Z_i=k)\right]
\left[
\log(\pi_k)+x_i\log(\lambda_k)-\lambda_k-\log(x_i!)
\right]
$$
$$
+\sum_{i=301}^{400}\left[
x_i\log(\lambda_2)-\lambda_2-\log(x_i!)
\right].
$$
Using the same responsibilities as in Problem 1,
$$
\tau_{ik}^0=P(Z_i=k\mid X_i=x_i,\theta^0),
$$
we obtain
$$
\boxed{
Q(\theta, \theta^0)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\sum_{k=1}^3\tau_{ik}^0
\left[
\log(\pi_k)+ x_i\log(\lambda_k)-\lambda_k-\log(x_i!)
\right]
+\sum_{i=301}^{400}
\left[
x_i\log(\lambda_2)-\lambda_2-\log(x_i!)
\right]
}
$$
The additional 100 labelled observations contribute directly to the terms involving $\lambda_2$, because their class membership is known and therefore no responsibility term is required.

### Part (b): E-step and M-step

For the first 300 unlabelled observations, the E-step is unchanged from Problem 1. The additional 100 observations have known class membership, so no responsibilities need to be calculated for them.

Thus, for $i=1,..,300$,
$$
\tau_{ik}^0=P(Z_i=k\mid X_i=x_i,\theta^0)=\frac{\pi_k^0(\lambda_k^0)^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_k^0}}{\sum_{j=1}^3\pi_j^0(\lambda_j^0)^{x_i}e^{-\lambda_j^0}},
\qquad
k=1,2,3.
$$
For the M-step, the updates for the mixture proportions are unchanged because the additional 100 labelled observations are modelled directly as $\text{Poisson}(\lambda_2)$ and do not contribute any terms involving $\pi_k$. Therefore,
$$
\pi_k^{\text{new}}=\frac{1}{300}\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{ik}^0, k=1,2,3.
$$
The update for $\lambda_1$ is also unchanged:
$$
\boxed{
\lambda_1^{\text{new}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i1}^0x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i1}^0}.
}
$$
Similarly, the update for $\lambda_3$ is unchanged:
$$
\boxed{
\lambda_3^{\text{new}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i3}^0x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i3}^0}.
}
$$
The update for $\lambda_2$ changes because both the unlabelled observations assigned probabilistically to class 2 and the 100 observations known to belong to class 2 contribute information about $\lambda_2$.
The terms in $Q(\theta,\theta^0)$ involving $\lambda_2$ are
$$
\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i2}^0(x_i\log\lambda_2-\lambda_2)+\sum_{i=301}^{400}(x_i\log\lambda_2-\lambda_2).
$$
Differentiating with respect to $\lambda_2$,
$$
\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\lambda_2}=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i2}^0
\left(\frac{x_i}{\lambda_2}-1\right)+\sum_{i=301}^{400}
\left(\frac{x_i}{\lambda_2}-1\right).
$$
Setting this equal to zero gives
$$
\frac{1}{\lambda_2}
\left[\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i2}^0x_i+\sum_{i=301}^{400}x_i
\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i2}^0+100.
$$
Hence,
$$
\boxed{
\lambda_2^{\text{new}}= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i2}^0x_i+\sum_{i=301}^{400}x_i}
{\sum_{i=1}^{300}\tau_{i2}^0+100}.
}
$$
Thus, $\lambda_2^{\text{new}}$ is a combined mean: the first 300 observations contribute according to their responsibilities for class 2, while each of the 100 labelled observations contributes with full weight because its class membership is known.

### Part (c): Implementation

The incomplete log-likelihood for the combined model is
$$
\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{300}\log
\left[\sum_{k=1}^3\pi_kf(x_i;\lambda_k)\right]+
\sum_{i=301}^{400}\log f(x_i;\lambda_2).
$$
I modified the EM implementation from Problem 1 to incorporate the 100 labelled class-2 observations. The E-step for the first 300 observations is unchanged. In the M-step, the updates for the mixture proportions, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_3$ are unchanged, while the update for $\lambda_2$ includes the additional labelled observations. The algorithm stops when either the absolute change in the incomplete log-likelihood is less than $10^{-5}$, or 100 EM iterations have been completed.
```{r}
compute.log.lik.2 <- function(X, X0, w.curr, lambda_curr) {
  prob.x.z <- compute.prob.x.z(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)$prob.x.z
  
  ill.unlabelled <- sum(log(rowSums(prob.x.z)))
  ill.labelled <- sum(dpois(X0, lambda_curr[2], log = TRUE))
  
  ill <- ill.unlabelled + ill.labelled
  
  return(list(ill = ill))
}

EM.iter.2 <- function(X, X0, w.curr, lambda_curr) {
  prob.x.z <- compute.prob.x.z(X, w.curr, lambda_curr)$prob.x.z
  
  P_ik <- prob.x.z / rowSums(prob.x.z)
  
  w.new <- colSums(P_ik) / sum(P_ik)
  
  lambda_new <- numeric(3)
  
  lambda_new[1] <- sum(P_ik[, 1] * X) / sum(P_ik[, 1])
  
  lambda_new[2] <- (sum(P_ik[, 2] * X) + sum(X0)) /
    (sum(P_ik[, 2]) + length(X0))
  
  lambda_new[3] <- sum(P_ik[, 3] * X) / sum(P_ik[, 3])
  
  return(list(w.new = w.new, lambda_new = lambda_new))
}
```
```{r}
mixture.EM.2 <- function(X, X0, w.init, lambda_init, epsilon = 1e-5, max.iter = 100) {
  w.curr <- w.init
  lambda_curr <- lambda_init
  
  log_liks <- c()
  
  log_liks <- c(log_liks, compute.log.lik.2(X, X0, w.curr, lambda_curr)$ill)
  
  delta.ll <- Inf
  n.iter <- 0
  
  while ((delta.ll > epsilon) & (n.iter < max.iter)) {
    EM.out <- EM.iter.2(X, X0, w.curr, lambda_curr)
    
    w.curr <- EM.out$w.new
    lambda_curr <- EM.out$lambda_new
    
    log_liks <- c(log_liks, compute.log.lik.2(X, X0, w.curr, lambda_curr)$ill)
    
    delta.ll <- abs(log_liks[length(log_liks)] -
                      log_liks[length(log_liks) - 1])
    
    n.iter <- n.iter + 1
  }
    
  return(list(w.curr = w.curr, lambda_curr = lambda_curr,
                log_liks = log_liks, n.iter = n.iter))
}
```
```{r}
EM1.2 <- mixture.EM.2(X, X0, w.init = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.4),
                      lambda_init = c(3, 20, 35))

EM2.2 <- mixture.EM.2(X, X0, w.init = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.7),
                      lambda_init = c(5, 25, 40))
```

```{r}

  xlab = "Iteration",
  ylab = "Incomplete log-likelihood",
  main = "Initialisation 2"
)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```

  )

For both initialisations, the incomplete log-likelihood increased monotonically at each EM iteration, as shown in the figure. The first run converged after 8 iterations, while the second run converged after 9 iterations. Both runs attained essentially the same final incomplete log-likelihood of -1429.048.

The resulting parameter estimates were
$$
\hat{\pi}_1=0.289,\qquad \hat{\pi}_2=0.281,\qquad \hat{\pi}_3=0.430,
$$
and
$$
\hat{\lambda}_1=5.87,\qquad \hat{\lambda}_2=19.86,\qquad \hat{\lambda}_3=37.85.
$$
Since both initialisations converged to essentially the same solution and achieved the same incomplete log-likelihood, either run gives the selected MLE estimates. The fitted model therefore suggests that approximately 29%, 28% and 43% of the unlabelled reef-season observations belong to the three latent classes, with typical seasonal counts of about 6, 20, and 38 coral trout, respectively.
